splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing constraints for actuarial assumption selection in calculating employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans under ERISA. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in such plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the end of the prior plan year (the statutory measurement date), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running during the period of absconding and the court retains jurisdiction to revoke.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release terms when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend the period beyond what Congress specified.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement when bringing successive collateral attacks on their convictions. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any claim they previously presented, in addition to Section 2255(h)'s requirements. If it does not apply, federal prisoners need only satisfy 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to Section 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive Section 2255 motions, imposing a categorical bar in addition to 2255(h) requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to Section 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar does not apply to federal prisoners filing Section 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy the requirements of Section 2255(h).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when and whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome could reshape how courts evaluate candidate standing to challenge election rules, potentially affecting rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election laws before an election takes place based on competitive injury from allegedly unlawful vote-counting rules.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack standing to challenge such laws pre-election because they cannot demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury traceable to the challenged law.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should take precedence over deference to agency interpretations in criminal and sentencing contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity. This split has become more salient after the Supreme Court's decisions in Kisor v. Wilkie and Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity, as one of the oldest canons of interpretation, takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to the Sentencing Commission's or agency's interpretation of ambiguous guidelines or criminal provisions takes priority over the rule of lenity.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds 'conspiring' and 'attempting' to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. This split affects career-offender designations and resulting sentence enhancements for many defendants.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a permissible interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight, so conspiracy and attempt qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision of the First Step Act. This determines whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, or if meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. The split leads to disparate sentencing outcomes depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is disqualifying, reading 'and' as 'or' or distributively in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes, alone or in combination with other factors, can support a sentence reduction, while others categorically foreclose reliance on non-retroactive changes in law. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to resolve this but has itself generated further disagreement about the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when revoking and resentencing, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the purposes of supervised release (breach of trust and deterrence) rather than retribution.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of a sentence imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits have held that revocation sentences must focus on the breach of trust and cannot serve retributive purposes.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for their supervised release violations, in addition to addressing the breach of trust.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of trust and the need to deter future violations, not retribution for the violating conduct itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state statute covers a substance not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) requires the state offense to involve a substance controlled under federal law or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-controlled substance suffices
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law regardless of whether the particular substance is also controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Must be federally controlled substance
positions.summary: Holds that to qualify as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines, the substance underlying the state conviction must also be controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an appeal from the denial of a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is governed by the civil appeal deadline (60 days for government party) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to civil appeal deadlines) or part of the criminal case (subject to criminal appeal deadlines). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, noting a lopsided circuit split on the issue.

positions.label: Civil appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline governs.

positions.label: Criminal appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case and thus governed by the shorter criminal appeal deadline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the benefit of the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with circuits that hold appreciation belongs to the debtor under § 348(f)(1)(A).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), coupled with the broad scope of § 541(a), means that post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor upon good-faith conversion, consistent with the statute's structure, policies, and legislative history designed to protect good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) rather than Bivens or other civil rights actions to challenge the conditions or terms of their confinement, including BOP decisions about earned time credits and prerelease custody under the First Step Act.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement), or whether civil rights actions remain available. This split has evolved over more than half a century and affects how prisoners can challenge BOP decisions about programming, credits, and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration-related challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration of confinement, such as the application of First Step Act earned time credits, must be brought through habeas corpus and cannot proceed as civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights actions (such as Bivens or § 1983) in addition to habeas corpus for challenges to conditions of confinement, even where the challenge may affect duration of custody.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal standards governing discrimination claims in hospitality and business contexts, indicating the Court found the approach sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review and suggesting a circuit split on the applicable standards.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied its own framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality establishments, which the Supreme Court found warranted review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different or conflicting standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the split that prompted certiorari.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether legal errors or constitutional claims that could have been raised in a § 2255 habeas petition may also serve as the basis for compassionate release. Some circuits permit courts to consider such claims as one factor, while others hold that compassionate release cannot be used as a substitute for habeas review.

positions.label: May consider conviction-related errors
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not be used as a vehicle to challenge the validity of a conviction or sentence, as those claims must be raised through § 2255 habeas proceedings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which bars states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any . . . broker,' preempts state negligence claims arising from a freight broker's selection of a motor carrier. This question affects liability in the trucking industry where brokers play a significant intermediary role.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted because they relate to the broker's 'service' of arranging transportation, which falls within the FAAAA's preemption clause.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers for negligent hiring of motor carriers are not preempted because they do not directly regulate brokers' prices, routes, or services within the meaning of the FAAAA.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to a person who uses marijuana.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users — particularly marijuana users — is consistent with the Second Amendment's text and historical tradition of firearms regulation.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) does not violate the Second Amendment because the historical tradition of firearms regulation supports disarming individuals whose drug use renders them dangerous or irresponsible.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a sufficient historical analogue justifying the disarmament of non-violent drug users.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
